title: What is Wrong With Assessment in Our Schools?
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles argues that school assessment systems should be criterion referenced, reporting what students actually know, rather than copying the norm-referenced ranking used by GCSEs and A levels. He opens with a thought experiment about doctors, pilots and builders, where what matters is whether they can do the job and ranking comes only after. He then shows the flaw in ranking with two sister schools teaching the same Spanish curriculum: one's students learn 75 percent and the other's 45 percent, yet norm-referenced data would look identical. The conclusion is that criterion assessment is the only form that tells a school whether its students can actually speak Spanish. It is Learning & Curriculum because the topic is assessment design.
points: Ranking is meaningless unless people can first do the thing that defines competence, as in medicine, flying and building.
Schools tend to copy GCSE norm referencing even though a different score can map to the same grade in different years.
Two schools with very different learning of the same curriculum can produce identical norm-referenced data.
A 75 versus 45 percent gap in curriculum learned equals three or four GCSE grades, which only criterion reporting reveals.
quotes: Our GCSEs and A levels are marked using criteria. But these are ignored when providing a grade. Scores are simply ranked and grades are awarded based on a distribution curve: norm referenced.
I would want to know, can the doctor diagnose me and treat me so that I get better? If none of the doctors can do this, but I have the one ranked first, I’m still going to die of cancer.
In real life we criterion reference. Then, if everyone passes the criterion, we might further select on rank – on norm referencing.
But in schools we muddy the water, because GCSEs and A levels are norm referenced from the get go, we tend to copy them.

If both schools rank by norm, they will have the same number of students in the top 25% and the bottom 25%, or in quintiles, or apportioned in 10ths – however you slice and dice them, their rankings will have the same distributions.
Well, which one is the school where students are likely to be able to speak Spanish? It’s obvious. It’s Star Academy.
That is why criterion assessment is always the better solution. It isn’t just for choosing doctors and pilots and nurses and builders.
